title: Name the term and show the instance
statement: For young students and novices, say the term and show a concrete instance of it together, never one without the other.
detail: An intro-video BrainLift for a Grade 3 reading course cites Ausubel (1968): elementary pupils and novices cannot process abstract propositions verbally without concrete and specific exemplars available at the same time or just before, and teaching that ignores this produces "rotely memorized and empty verbalisms" (`downloads/BrainLift - What makes a good intro video.md`, line 455). Its narration rule is to name the term and show the instance together, and never the instance alone either, because compression strips the terms first and a scene of two animals is not yet the characters until somebody says so (line 319). The source gives no DOI or link for the 1968 work.
against: A later run found: A reading unit's opening film shows an idea in two beats without its technical term, on purpose, because a later lesson names it, and lesson research for the unit held that the later lesson attaches the name better to a concept learners already hold. That is the instance before the term, which this record rules out; the new record Teach the idea before its name carries the rule (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/video/u1-script-and-visual-plan.md`).

two beats gesture at xenia, treating a stranger who knocks as its own test, without using the word "xenia" itself, since the word is not introduced until `U1T6`

One decision this raises: do not give the child the Greek word xenia at L2. The graph reserves the naming for L6, and R-KC-5 wants prior knowledge reused rather than re-taught, which works better if L6 gets to attach a new name to a concept the child already holds.

a step between the quote and the definition: "Othello never hears it · We do"
Othello never hears this. We do. That is dramatic irony: the audience knows something a character doesn’t.
